newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu tours bombed market before talks.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu tours bombed market before talks.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu lit memorial candles in a bomb-ravaged Jerusalem market on Wednesday before talks with a high-level Jordanian team seeking to lower Israeli-PLO tensions.
The right-wing leader visited Mahane Yehuda market a week after the blasts and demanded Palestinian President Yasser Arafat crack down on Moslem militants.

"The fact that the Palestinian Authority has failed in its obligations to fight terrorism has resulted in these events," Netanyahu said during a 30-minute walk through the street market where 15 people, including the bombers, were killed.

King Hussein's brother Crown Prince Hassan and Jordanian Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali were due to meet Netanyahu in his Jerusalem office as part of a peace mission following Egyptian efforts to lower tensions in the region.
Netanyahu is due to visit King Hussein in Jordan next week.

"In (Wednesday's) discussions, there will be no talk...about advancing the peace process until Israel is convinced the Palestinian Authority has begun to fulfil its commitments to fight terrorism," said Israeli Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh.

"All we are asking is that the Jordanian delegation convince the Palestinians that they, the Palestinians, should do exactly what the Jordanians are doing and that is fighting terrorism," Netanyahu's communications director David Bar-Illan said.

Netanyahu shook hands with shop owners in the market -- an election stomping ground for right-wing Israeli politicians -- and put on a religious skullcap while lighting a candle and saying a prayer for the dead.

"Bibi, Bibi," the crowd chanted, using Netanyahu's nickname in a sign of support for the Likud party leader who won election last year by pledging to boost security in the wake of a series of suicide bombings that killed 57 people.

"The people of Israel overwhelmingly support the stand of this government...We expect reciprocity. We expect the Palestinians to fight terrorism. The people in this market suffered a terrible massacre. They are the first people to support this firm policy," he said.

"The decisive majority of the public in Israel are not ready to accept a one-sided process in which attackers are sent from the territories of the Palestinian Authority or by headquarters there and let it pass quietly. We won't let it pass quietly," Netanyahu said.
Israel closed the West Bank and Gaza after the twin bombing, stopping tens of thousands of Arab workers from reaching their jobs in Israel, paralysing trade and shutting down factories.
Israeli troops arrested another 20 Palestinians in the West Bank overnight, bringing to more than 170 the number detained since the attack.
Palestinians have said the Israeli measures are collective punishments that weaken Arafat and strengthen extremist forces.
The Israeli army said on Wednesday it was allowing Palestinians to return to work in Jewish settlements in the West Bank and Gaza.
In addition, the army said it would let "vital supplies" into the Gaza Strip.
"We emphasise the full closure is continuing and the entry of Palestinian workers into Israel is still banned," the military said in a statement.

In Cairo on Tuesday, Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak said after meeting Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy that Israel should continue talks with the Palestinians because peace was the only way to avoid further terrorism.

The Egyptian leader, responding to Israel's calls for Arafat to act against anti-Israeli militants, said the Palestinian leader was not "powerful enough" to implement the tough measures Israel demanded of him.
While the security stalemate continued, the military wing of the Islamic militant group Hamas pledged more suicide attacks.
"A chain of martyrdom attacks will come at the appropriate time to hit deep into Zionism," the Izz el-Deen al-Qassam Brigades said in a statement faxed to Reuters in Jerusalem on Tuesday.
